nodes.name: q is an even prime power
nodes.statement: Throughout this paper, except Section~3, $q$ is an even power of a prime number $p$.
nodes.statement_short: Except in Section 3, $q$ is an even power of a prime $p$.

nodes.name: Hermitian variety
nodes.statement: A Hermitian variety over ${\Bbb F}_q$ is a hypersurface in ${\Bbb P^n}$ defined by \begin{equation} (X_0^{\sqrt{q}}, \dots , X_n^{\sqrt{q}}) A \, {}^t\!(X_0, \dots , X_n) =0, \end{equation} where $A$ is a square matrix of order $n+1$ whose entries are in ${\Bbb F}_q$ with the property ${}^t\!A=A^{(\sqrt{q})}$; here $A^{(\sqrt{q})}$ means taking entry-wise the $\sqrt{q}$-th power, and ${}^t\!A$ is the transposed matrix of $A$.
differentia: where $A$ is a square matrix of order $n+1$ whose entries are in ${\Bbb F}_q$ with the property ${}^t\!A=A^{(\sqrt{q})}$
nodes.statement_short: A Hermitian variety is the hypersurface $(X^{\sqrt q})A\,{}^tX=0$ with ${}^tA=A^{(\sqrt q)}$.

nodes.name: Hermitian equation
nodes.statement: (X_0^{\sqrt{q}}, \dots , X_n^{\sqrt{q}}) A \, {}^t\!(X_0, \dots , X_n) =0,
nodes.label: def_hermitian

nodes.name: Hermitian polynomial
nodes.statement: We refer this kind of polynomial as a Hermitian polynomial over ${\Bbb F}_q$.

nodes.name: Hermitian hypersurface of degree sqrt(q)+1
nodes.statement: For a homogeneous polynomial $F$ of degree $\sqrt{q}+1$ whose coefficients are in ${\Bbb F}_q$, the hypersurface given by $F=0$ is Hermitian if and only if there is an element $\rho \in {\Bbb F}_q^{\ast}$ such that $\rho F$ is a Hermitian polynomial.
nodes.statement_short: A degree-$(\sqrt q+1)$ hypersurface $F=0$ is Hermitian iff some nonzero scalar multiple of $F$ is a Hermitian polynomial.

nodes.name: Hermitian polynomials form a vector space
nodes.statement: The family of Hermitian polynomials over ${\Bbb F}_q$ forms an ${\Bbb F}_{\! \sqrt{q}}$ vector space.
conclusions: The family of Hermitian polynomials over ${\Bbb F}_q$ forms an ${\Bbb F}_{\! \sqrt{q}}$ vector space.

nodes.name: Nonsingularity criterion for Hermitian varieties
nodes.statement: It is obvious that the Hermitian polynomial (\ref{def_hermitian}) defines a nonsingular Hermitian variety if and only if $\det A \neq 0$.
assumptions: the Hermitian polynomial (\ref{def_hermitian})
conclusions: defines a nonsingular Hermitian variety if and only if $\det A \neq 0$

nodes.name: Standard form of a nonsingular Hermitian variety
nodes.statement: By the standard argument, a nonsingular Hermitian variety is projectively equivalent to the variety \begin{equation} H_{n-1} : X_0^{\sqrt{q}+1} + X_1^{\sqrt{q}+1} + \dots + X_n^{\sqrt{q}+1} =0 \end{equation} over ${\Bbb F}_q$.
assumptions: a nonsingular Hermitian variety
conclusions: is projectively equivalent to the variety
nodes.statement_short: Every nonsingular Hermitian variety is projectively equivalent to the Fermat-type $H_{n-1}: \sum X_i^{\sqrt q+1}=0$.

nodes.name: Weil-Deligne bound
nodes.statement: The Weil conjecture \cite{wei1949} established by Deligne \cite{del1973} implies that the number $N$ of ${\Bbb F}_q$-points of a nonsingular hypersurface of degree $d$ in ${\Bbb P}^n$ defined over ${\Bbb F}_q$ is bounded by \begin{equation} N \leq \frac{q^n -1}{q-1} + \frac{d-1}{d} \left( (d-1)^n - (-1)^n \right) \sqrt{q}^{n-1}. \end{equation}
assumptions: a nonsingular hypersurface of degree $d$ in ${\Bbb P}^n$ defined over ${\Bbb F}_q$
conclusions: is bounded by
nodes.statement_short: A nonsingular degree-$d$ hypersurface in $\mathbb P^n$ has at most $\frac{q^n-1}{q-1}+\frac{d-1}{d}((d-1)^n-(-1)^n)\sqrt q^{n-1}$ points.

nodes.name: Weil-Deligne inequality
nodes.statement: N \leq \frac{q^n -1}{q-1} + \frac{d-1}{d} \left( (d-1)^n - (-1)^n \right) \sqrt{q}^{n-1}.
nodes.label: weil_deligne

nodes.name: Equality in the Weil-Deligne bound forces d <= sqrt(q)+1
nodes.statement: Furthermore, if equality holds in (\ref{weil_deligne}) for a certain nonsingular hypersurface of degree $d$, then $d \leq \sqrt{q}+1$.
assumptions: if equality holds in (\ref{weil_deligne}) for a certain nonsingular hypersurface of degree $d$
conclusions: then $d \leq \sqrt{q}+1$.

nodes.name: Hermitian variety attains the Weil-Deligne bound
nodes.statement: The number $N_q(H_{n-1})$ achieves the equality in (\ref{weil_deligne}) for $d=\sqrt{q} +1$.
assumptions: for $d=\sqrt{q} +1$
conclusions: The number $N_q(H_{n-1})$ achieves the equality in (\ref{weil_deligne})

nodes.name: Number of points of the Hermitian curve
nodes.statement: Note that $N_q(H_{1}) = \sqrt{q}^3 +1$.

nodes.name: Hirschfeld-Storme-Thas-Voloch theorem
nodes.statement: Suppose that $q \neq 4$. Let $C$ be a plane curve over ${\Bbb F}_q$ of degree $\sqrt{q} +1$ without ${\Bbb F}_q$-line components. If $C$ has $\sqrt{q}^3 +1$ points over ${\Bbb F}_q$, then $C$ is a Hermitian curve.
assumptions: Suppose that $q \neq 4$.
Let $C$ be a plane curve over ${\Bbb F}_q$ of degree $\sqrt{q} +1$ without ${\Bbb F}_q$-line components.
If $C$ has $\sqrt{q}^3 +1$ points over ${\Bbb F}_q$,
conclusions: then $C$ is a Hermitian curve.
nodes.statement_short: For $q\ne4$, a plane curve of degree $\sqrt q+1$ without $\mathbb F_q$-lines having $\sqrt q^3+1$ points is Hermitian.
nodes.label: hermitiancurve

nodes.name: Characterization of Hermitian surfaces by the number of points
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a surface in ${\Bbb P}^3$ defined over ${\Bbb F}_q$ without ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane components. If the degree of $S$ is $\sqrt{q}+1$ and $N_q(S) = (\sqrt{q}^3+1)(q+1)$, then $S$ is a nonsingular Hermitian surface over ${\Bbb F}_q$.
assumptions: Let $S$ be a surface in ${\Bbb P}^3$ defined over ${\Bbb F}_q$ without ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane components.
If the degree of $S$ is $\sqrt{q}+1$ and $N_q(S) = (\sqrt{q}^3+1)(q+1)$,
conclusions: then $S$ is a nonsingular Hermitian surface over ${\Bbb F}_q$.
nodes.statement_short: A surface of degree $\sqrt q+1$ in $\mathbb P^3$ without $\mathbb F_q$-planes with $(\sqrt q^3+1)(q+1)$ points is a nonsingular Hermitian surface.
nodes.label: maintheorem

nodes.name: Notation: N_q(X), local intersection multiplicity, tangent line
nodes.statement: \begin{itemize} \item When $X$ is an algebraic set in ${\Bbb P}^n$ defined by equations over ${\Bbb F}_q$, the set of ${\Bbb F}_q$-points in $X$ is denoted by $X({\Bbb F}_q)$, and the cardinality of $X({\Bbb F}_q)$ by $N_q(X)$. \item When coordinates $X_0, \dots , X_n$ of ${\Bbb P}^n$ are given, for a homogeneous polynomial $h$ in those variables, $\{ h=0 \}$ means the hypersurface defined by $h=0$. \item Let $D$ and $E$ are curves in ${\Bbb P}^2$ without common components. For a point $Q \in D\cap E$, $i(D.E;Q)$ denotes the local intersection multiplicity of $D$ and $E$ at $Q$, and $(D.E) = \sum_{Q \in D \cap E} i(D.E;Q)$. \item For a plane curve $C \subset {\Bbb P}^2$ and a nonsingular point $P \in C$, $T_P(C)$ denotes the embedded tangent line to $C$ at $P$. \item The multiplicative set ${\Bbb F}_q \setminus \{0\}$ is denoted by ${\Bbb F}_q^{\ast}$. \item For a finite set $Y$, ${}^{\#}Y$ denotes the number of elements of $Y$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Notation: $X(\mathbb F_q)$, $N_q(X)$, $\{h=0\}$, $i(D.E;Q)$, $(D.E)$, $T_P(C)$, $\mathbb F_q^*$, ${}^\#Y$.

nodes.name: Sziklai bound
nodes.statement: Let $d$ be an integer with $2 \leq d \leq q+2$, and $C$ a curve of degree $d$ in ${\Bbb P}^2$ defined over ${\Bbb F}_q$ without ${\Bbb F}_q$-linear components. Then \begin{equation} N_q(C) \leq (d-1)q+1 \end{equation} except for curves over ${\Bbb F}_4$ which are projectively equivalent to the curve defined by \[ K: \ (X_0 + X_1 + X_2)^4 + (X_0X_1 + X_1X_2 +X_2X_0)^2 +X_0X_1X_2(X_0 + X_1 + X_2) =0. \] For the exceptional curve $K$ above, $N_4(K)=14$.
assumptions: Let $d$ be an integer with $2 \leq d \leq q+2$, and $C$ a curve of degree $d$ in ${\Bbb P}^2$ defined over ${\Bbb F}_q$ without ${\Bbb F}_q$-linear components.
conclusions: N_q(C) \leq (d-1)q+1
For the exceptional curve $K$ above, $N_4(K)=14$.
nodes.statement_short: A plane curve of degree $d$ without $\mathbb F_q$-lines has $N_q(C)\le(d-1)q+1$, except one curve $K$ over $\mathbb F_4$ with 14 points.
nodes.label: sziklai_bound

nodes.name: Sziklai inequality
nodes.statement: N_q(C) \leq (d-1)q+1
nodes.label: ineq_sziklai_bound

nodes.name: Hermitian curve attains the Sziklai bound
nodes.statement: The number $N_q(H_1)$ attains the equality of the Sziklai bound too.
conclusions: The number $N_q(H_1)$ attains the equality of the Sziklai bound

nodes.name: Absolute irreducibility criterion for plane curves
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a curve over ${\Bbb F}_q$ of degree $d$ in ${\Bbb P}^2$ without ${\Bbb F}_q$-linear components. If $N_q(C) \geq (d-2)q +3$, then $C$ is absolutely irreducible.
assumptions: Let $C$ be a curve over ${\Bbb F}_q$ of degree $d$ in ${\Bbb P}^2$ without ${\Bbb F}_q$-linear components.
If $N_q(C) \geq (d-2)q +3$,
conclusions: then $C$ is absolutely irreducible.
nodes.label: absolutelyirreducible

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2.2
nodes.statement: \noindent \mbox{\em Proof.\hspace*{2mm}} First note that the range of $d$ is $2 \leq d \leq q+2$ by assumptions. (Step~1) Suppose $C$ is decomposed into two curves $C_1$ and $C_2$ over ${\Bbb F}_q$. For each $i =1, 2$, let $d_i$ be the degree of $C_i$. If either ``$q\neq 4$" or ``$q=4$ and none of the $C_i$'s is projectively equivalent to $K$," then \[ N_q(C) \leq N_q(C_1)+N_q(C_2) \leq ((d_1-1)q + 1) +((d_2-1)q + 1) \leq (d-2)q + 2. \] We consider the exceptional case, namely ``$q=4$ and one of the $C_i$'s is projectively equivalent to $K$ oner ${\Bbb F}_4$." Applying an ${\Bbb F}_4$-linear transformation if necessary, we may assume that $C_1=K$. Then $d=6$ and $d_2=2$, because $2 \leq d \leq 6$ and $C$ has no ${\Bbb F}_4$-linear components. Since $C_2$ is ${\Bbb F}_4$-irreducible of degree $2$, $N_4(C_2) =5$ or $1$. When $N_4(C_2) =1$, $N_4(C) \leq 14 +1 < (6-2)4 + 3.$ If $C_2$ is an absolutely irreducible conic, then ${}^{\#}(C_2 \cap \mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{F}_2)) \leq 4$, because the maximum length of $\mathbb{F}_2$-arc is $4$. Since $K(\mathbb{F}_4) = \mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{F}_4) \setminus \mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{F}_2)$ (see \cite[\S 3]{hom-kim2009}), ${}^{\#}(K(\mathbb{F}_4) \cap C_2(\mathbb{F}_4))\geq 1$. Hence $N_q(C) \leq 14 + 5 -1 = (6-2)4+2.$ Therefore $C$ is irreducible over ${\Bbb F}_q$. (Step~2) Suppose that the ${\Bbb F}_q$-irreducible curve $C$ is not absolutely irreducible. Let $D$ be an irreducible component of $C$. Then $D$ is defined over an extension $\mathbb{F}_{q^t}$ of $\mathbb{F}_q$ with $t \geq 2$, and $C= D \cup D^{(q)} \cup \dots \cup D^{(q^{t-1})}$, where $D^{(q)}, \dots , D^{(q^{t-1})}$ are conjugates of $D$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$. Hence $C({\Bbb F}_q) \subset D \cap D^{(q)}$ and $\deg D = \deg D^{(q)} \leq \frac{d}{2}.$ Hence $N_q(C) \leq \left( \frac{d}{2}\right)^2$. Since $2 \leq d \leq q+2$, we have $\left( \frac{d}{2}\right)^2< (d-2)q + 3$. Indeed, consider the quadratic $P(d) = \left( \frac{d}{2}\right)^2 - (d-2)q - 3.$ Then $P(2)<0$ and $P(q+2)<0$, which implies $P(d)<0$ for any $d$ with $2 \leq d \leq q+2$. Therefore the curve $C$ is absolutely irreducible too. \hfill \mbox{$ \Box $}
nodes.statement_short: Rule out an $\mathbb F_q$-decomposition via the Sziklai bound (special care for $K$ over $\mathbb F_4$), then rule out conjugate components by $N_q(C)\le(d/2)^2$.

nodes.name: Step 1: irreducible over F_q
nodes.statement: (Step~1) Suppose $C$ is decomposed into two curves $C_1$ and $C_2$ over ${\Bbb F}_q$. For each $i =1, 2$, let $d_i$ be the degree of $C_i$. If either ``$q\neq 4$" or ``$q=4$ and none of the $C_i$'s is projectively equivalent to $K$," then \[ N_q(C) \leq N_q(C_1)+N_q(C_2) \leq ((d_1-1)q + 1) +((d_2-1)q + 1) \leq (d-2)q + 2. \] We consider the exceptional case, namely ``$q=4$ and one of the $C_i$'s is projectively equivalent to $K$ oner ${\Bbb F}_4$." Applying an ${\Bbb F}_4$-linear transformation if necessary, we may assume that $C_1=K$. Then $d=6$ and $d_2=2$, because $2 \leq d \leq 6$ and $C$ has no ${\Bbb F}_4$-linear components. Since $C_2$ is ${\Bbb F}_4$-irreducible of degree $2$, $N_4(C_2) =5$ or $1$. When $N_4(C_2) =1$, $N_4(C) \leq 14 +1 < (6-2)4 + 3.$ If $C_2$ is an absolutely irreducible conic, then ${}^{\#}(C_2 \cap \mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{F}_2)) \leq 4$, because the maximum length of $\mathbb{F}_2$-arc is $4$. Since $K(\mathbb{F}_4) = \mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{F}_4) \setminus \mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{F}_2)$ (see \cite[\S 3]{hom-kim2009}), ${}^{\#}(K(\mathbb{F}_4) \cap C_2(\mathbb{F}_4))\geq 1$. Hence $N_q(C) \leq 14 + 5 -1 = (6-2)4+2.$ Therefore $C$ is irreducible over ${\Bbb F}_q$.
nodes.statement_short: Show $C$ is $\mathbb F_q$-irreducible.

nodes.name: Generic decomposition case
nodes.statement: (Step~1) Suppose $C$ is decomposed into two curves $C_1$ and $C_2$ over ${\Bbb F}_q$. For each $i =1, 2$, let $d_i$ be the degree of $C_i$. If either ``$q\neq 4$" or ``$q=4$ and none of the $C_i$'s is projectively equivalent to $K$," then \[ N_q(C) \leq N_q(C_1)+N_q(C_2) \leq ((d_1-1)q + 1) +((d_2-1)q + 1) \leq (d-2)q + 2. \]
nodes.statement_short: If no component is $K$, the Sziklai bound gives $N_q(C)\le(d-2)q+2$.

nodes.name: Exceptional case with K
nodes.statement: We consider the exceptional case, namely ``$q=4$ and one of the $C_i$'s is projectively equivalent to $K$ oner ${\Bbb F}_4$." Applying an ${\Bbb F}_4$-linear transformation if necessary, we may assume that $C_1=K$. Then $d=6$ and $d_2=2$, because $2 \leq d \leq 6$ and $C$ has no ${\Bbb F}_4$-linear components. Since $C_2$ is ${\Bbb F}_4$-irreducible of degree $2$, $N_4(C_2) =5$ or $1$. When $N_4(C_2) =1$, $N_4(C) \leq 14 +1 < (6-2)4 + 3.$ If $C_2$ is an absolutely irreducible conic, then ${}^{\#}(C_2 \cap \mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{F}_2)) \leq 4$, because the maximum length of $\mathbb{F}_2$-arc is $4$. Since $K(\mathbb{F}_4) = \mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{F}_4) \setminus \mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{F}_2)$ (see \cite[\S 3]{hom-kim2009}), ${}^{\#}(K(\mathbb{F}_4) \cap C_2(\mathbb{F}_4))\geq 1$. Hence $N_q(C) \leq 14 + 5 -1 = (6-2)4+2.$
nodes.statement_short: If $q=4$ and $C_1=K$, count conic points to get $N_4(C)\le(6-2)4+2$.

nodes.name: Conclude F_q-irreducibility
nodes.statement: Therefore $C$ is irreducible over ${\Bbb F}_q$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $C$ is irreducible over $\mathbb F_q$.

nodes.name: Step 2: absolutely irreducible
nodes.statement: (Step~2) Suppose that the ${\Bbb F}_q$-irreducible curve $C$ is not absolutely irreducible. Let $D$ be an irreducible component of $C$. Then $D$ is defined over an extension $\mathbb{F}_{q^t}$ of $\mathbb{F}_q$ with $t \geq 2$, and $C= D \cup D^{(q)} \cup \dots \cup D^{(q^{t-1})}$, where $D^{(q)}, \dots , D^{(q^{t-1})}$ are conjugates of $D$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$. Hence $C({\Bbb F}_q) \subset D \cap D^{(q)}$ and $\deg D = \deg D^{(q)} \leq \frac{d}{2}.$ Hence $N_q(C) \leq \left( \frac{d}{2}\right)^2$. Since $2 \leq d \leq q+2$, we have $\left( \frac{d}{2}\right)^2< (d-2)q + 3$. Indeed, consider the quadratic $P(d) = \left( \frac{d}{2}\right)^2 - (d-2)q - 3.$ Then $P(2)<0$ and $P(q+2)<0$, which implies $P(d)<0$ for any $d$ with $2 \leq d \leq q+2$. Therefore the curve $C$ is absolutely irreducible too. \hfill \mbox{$ \Box $}
nodes.statement_short: Rule out a decomposition into Galois-conjugate components.

nodes.name: Conjugate components
nodes.statement: (Step~2) Suppose that the ${\Bbb F}_q$-irreducible curve $C$ is not absolutely irreducible. Let $D$ be an irreducible component of $C$. Then $D$ is defined over an extension $\mathbb{F}_{q^t}$ of $\mathbb{F}_q$ with $t \geq 2$, and $C= D \cup D^{(q)} \cup \dots \cup D^{(q^{t-1})}$, where $D^{(q)}, \dots , D^{(q^{t-1})}$ are conjugates of $D$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$. Hence $C({\Bbb F}_q) \subset D \cap D^{(q)}$ and $\deg D = \deg D^{(q)} \leq \frac{d}{2}.$ Hence $N_q(C) \leq \left( \frac{d}{2}\right)^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Conjugate components force $N_q(C)\le(d/2)^2$.

nodes.name: Quadratic comparison
nodes.statement: Since $2 \leq d \leq q+2$, we have $\left( \frac{d}{2}\right)^2< (d-2)q + 3$. Indeed, consider the quadratic $P(d) = \left( \frac{d}{2}\right)^2 - (d-2)q - 3.$ Then $P(2)<0$ and $P(q+2)<0$, which implies $P(d)<0$ for any $d$ with $2 \leq d \leq q+2$.
nodes.statement_short: Show $(d/2)^2<(d-2)q+3$ via a quadratic in $d$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore the curve $C$ is absolutely irreducible too. \hfill \mbox{$ \Box $}
nodes.statement_short: Hence $C$ is absolutely irreducible.

nodes.name: Plane cubics over F_4 with 9 points
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a plane curve of degree $3$ over $\mathbb{F}_4$ without $\mathbb{F}_4$-linear components. Suppose $N_4(C)=9$. Then $C$ is absolutely irreducible and all $\mathbb{F}_4$-points are nonsingular. In addition, suppose that all $\mathbb{F}_4$-points are flexes, i.e., $i(T_p(C).C;P) =3$ for any $P \in C(\mathbb{F}_4)$. Then $C$ is a Hermitian curve.
assumptions: Let $C$ be a plane curve of degree $3$ over $\mathbb{F}_4$ without $\mathbb{F}_4$-linear components.
Suppose $N_4(C)=9$.
In addition, suppose that all $\mathbb{F}_4$-points are flexes, i.e., $i(T_p(C).C;P) =3$ for any $P \in C(\mathbb{F}_4)$.
conclusions: Then $C$ is absolutely irreducible and all $\mathbb{F}_4$-points are nonsingular.
Then $C$ is a Hermitian curve.
nodes.statement_short: A cubic over $\mathbb F_4$ with 9 points is absolutely irreducible and smooth at its points; if all points are flexes it is Hermitian.

Since  egin{gather} F(X_0, X_1, 0) = c_2(X_0^3 + X_1^3) \ \ (c_2 \in \mathbb{F}_4^{\ast})

nodes.name: Segre's lemma
nodes.statement: Let $d$ be an integer with $1 \leq d \leq q+1$, and $C$ be a curve of degree $d$ in ${\Bbb P}^2$ defined over ${\Bbb F}_q$, which may have ${\Bbb F}_q$-linear components. Then $N_q(C) \leq dq+1$, and equality holds if and only if $C$ is a pencil of $d$ ${\Bbb F}_q$-lines.

nodes.name: Elementary bound
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a surface of degree $d$ in ${\Bbb P}^3$ defined over ${\Bbb F}_q$ without ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane components. Then \begin{equation} N_q(S) \leq (d-1)q^2 + dq +1. \end{equation}

conclusions: N_q(S) \leq (d-1)q^2 + dq +1.

nodes.statement_short: $S$ is a degree-$d$ surface ($2\le d\le q+1$) without $\mathbb F_q$-planes attaining the elementary bound.

conclusions: The surface $S$ contains an ${\Bbb F}_q$-line.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.3
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: without $\mathbb F_q$-lines every plane section obeys the Sziklai bound, and Homma's $s$-degree bound then caps $N_q(S)$ below the elementary bound.

nodes.name: Assume no F_q-lines
nodes.statement: \noindent \mbox{\em Proof.\hspace*{2mm}} Suppose $S$ does not contain any ${\Bbb F}_q$-lines. Let $H$ be any ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane in ${\Bbb P}^3$. Then $S\cap H$ is a plane curve of degree $d$ over ${\Bbb F}_q$ in $H = {\Bbb P}^2$, and has no ${\Bbb F}_q$-line as a component.
nodes.statement_short: Suppose $S$ has no $\mathbb F_q$-lines; plane sections then have no line components.

nodes.name: Bound plane sections
nodes.statement: Hence \begin{equation} N_q(S\cap H) \leq \left\{ \begin{array}{cl} (d-1)q +1 & \mbox{\rm if $(d,q) \neq (4,4)$}\\ 14 & \mbox{\rm if $(d,q) = (4,4)$} \end{array} \right. \end{equation} by Lemma~\ref{sziklai_bound}.
nodes.statement_short: Bound each plane section by the Sziklai bound.

nodes.name: s-degree bound
nodes.statement: In a term of \cite{hom2012}, defining the $s$-degree $\delta$ of $S({\Bbb F}_q)$ by \[ \delta = \max \{ N_q(S\cap H) \mid \mbox{\rm $H$ is an ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane} \}, \] we have \[ N_q(S) \leq (\delta -1)q + 1 + \left\lfloor \frac{\delta -1}{q +1} \right\rfloor \] by \cite[Proposition 2.2]{hom2012}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Homma's bound in terms of the $s$-degree $\delta$.

nodes.name: Compute the bound
nodes.statement: Hence if $(d,q) \neq (4,4)$, then \begin{eqnarray*} N_q(S) & \leq & (d-1)q^2 +1 + \left\lfloor \frac{(d -1)q}{q +1} \right\rfloor\\ &=& (d-1)q^2 +1 + \left\lfloor \frac{(d -2)(q+1)+q+2-d}{q +1} \right\rfloor\\ &=& (d-1)(q^2+1) \, {\rm ;} \end{eqnarray*} and if $(d,q) = (4,4)$, then $N_q(S) \leq 55$.

nodes.name: Verification of (alpha)
nodes.statement: {\em The verification of} ($\alpha$). If $S \cap K$ contains an ${\Bbb F}_q$-line, then it must be a planar ${\Bbb F}_q$-pencil by (i). Since $Q$ is a point of $S$, there is an ${\Bbb F}_q$-line $m$ passing through $Q$ among $d$ lines of $S \cap K$. Hence $l$ and $m$ spans an ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane which is one of the $H_i$'s, say $H_i$. Then $v_i \in l \cap m =\{ Q \}$, which contradicts to the choice of $Q$.
nodes.statement_short: A line in $S\cap K$ through $Q$ would make $Q$ a vertex.

nodes.name: Verification of (beta)
nodes.statement: {\em The verification of} ($\beta$). Let $Q_{i,j}$ be the intersection point of $l_{i,j}$ with $K$. Then the plane containing $l$ and $Q_{i,j}$ is $H_i$ and the line containing $v_i$ and $Q_{i,j}$ is $l_{i,j}$. Hence $Q_{i,j} =Q_{i',j'}$ implies $(i,j) = (i',j')$. Since \[ (S\cap K)({\Bbb F}_q) \supset \{Q_{i,j} \mid 1 \leq i \leq q+1, \, 1 \leq j \leq d-1 \} \cup \{Q\}, \] we have $N_q(S\cap K) \geq (d-1)(q+1) +1.$ \hfill \mbox{$ \Box $}
nodes.statement_short: The points $Q_{i,j}=l_{i,j}\cap K$ are distinct, giving ($\beta$).

nodes.name: Lines through a pencil vertex lie in the pencil
nodes.statement: Let $H$ be an ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane such that $S \cap H$ is a planar ${\Bbb F}_q$-pencil of degree $d$. If an ${\Bbb F}_q$-line $l \subset S$ passes through $v_{S\cap H}$, then $l$ is a component of $S \cap H$.
assumptions: Let $H$ be an ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane such that $S \cap H$ is a planar ${\Bbb F}_q$-pencil of degree $d$.
If an ${\Bbb F}_q$-line $l \subset S$ passes through $v_{S\cap H}$,
conclusions: then $l$ is a component of $S \cap H$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.7
nodes.statement: \noindent \mbox{\em Proof.\hspace*{2mm}} Since $d \geq 2$, there are two distinct components $l_1$ and $l_2$ of $S \cap H$. Suppose that $l$ is not contained in $H$. Then $l$ and $l_i$ span an ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane, say $H_i$. Hence $S\cap H_i$ is also a planar ${\Bbb F}_q$-pencil of degree $d$ by Lemma~\ref{planar_pencil}~(i). By the construction of $H_1$ and $H_2$, \[ v_{S \cap H_1} = l \cap l_1 = v_{S \cap H} = l \cap l_2 = v_{S \cap H_2}, \] which contradicts (ii) of Lemma~\ref{planar_pencil}. Hence $l$ is contained in $H$, and hence it is a component of $S\cap H$. \hfill \mbox{$ \Box $}
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: if $l\not\subset H$, planes spanned by $l$ and two pencil lines share a vertex, contradicting Lemma 3.6 (ii).

nodes.name: Two components
nodes.statement: \noindent \mbox{\em Proof.\hspace*{2mm}} Since $d \geq 2$, there are two distinct components $l_1$ and $l_2$ of $S \cap H$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick two components $l_1,l_2$ of the pencil.

nodes.name: Planes through l
nodes.statement: Suppose that $l$ is not contained in $H$. Then $l$ and $l_i$ span an ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane, say $H_i$. Hence $S\cap H_i$ is also a planar ${\Bbb F}_q$-pencil of degree $d$ by Lemma~\ref{planar_pencil}~(i).
nodes.statement_short: If $l\not\subset H$, the planes $H_i=\langle l,l_i\rangle$ cut pencils.

nodes.name: Equal vertices
nodes.statement: By the construction of $H_1$ and $H_2$, \[ v_{S \cap H_1} = l \cap l_1 = v_{S \cap H} = l \cap l_2 = v_{S \cap H_2}, \] which contradicts (ii) of Lemma~\ref{planar_pencil}.
nodes.statement_short: Both pencils have the same vertex, contradicting injectivity.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Hence $l$ is contained in $H$, and hence it is a component of $S\cap H$. \hfill \mbox{$ \Box $}
nodes.statement_short: So $l\subset H$.

nodes.name: Unique pencil plane with given vertex
nodes.statement: For any ${\Bbb F}_q$-point $P$ of $S$, there is a unique ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane $H$ such that $S\cap H$ is a planar ${\Bbb F}_q$-pencil of degree $d$ with $v_{S\cap H} =P$.
assumptions: For any ${\Bbb F}_q$-point $P$ of $S$,
conclusions: there is a unique ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane $H$ such that $S\cap H$ is a planar ${\Bbb F}_q$-pencil of degree $d$ with $v_{S\cap H} =P$.
nodes.label: bijective_pencil_point

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 3.8
nodes.statement: \noindent \mbox{\em Proof.\hspace*{2mm}} From Lemma~\ref{contains_line} and Lemma~\ref{planar_pencil} (i), there is a line $l$ on $S$ containing $P$. Indeed the existence of an ${\Bbb F}_q$-line $l'$ on $S$ is guaranteed by Lemma~\ref{contains_line}; if the point $P$ in question lies on $l'$, there is nothing to do; when $P \not\in l'$, consider the ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane $H'$ containing $l'$ and $P$, then $S \cap H'$ is a planar ${\Bbb F}_q$-pencil by Lemma~\ref{planar_pencil} (i), which contains $P$; hence there is a line $l$ on $S$ containing $P$. Hence, by (ii) of Lemma~\ref{planar_pencil} there is a desired ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane, and such a plane is uniquely determined by $P$. \hfill \mbox{$ \Box $}
nodes.statement_short: Find a line on $S$ through $P$ via Lemmas 3.3 and 3.6 (i), then apply the bijection of Lemma 3.6 (ii).

nodes.name: Line through P
nodes.statement: \noindent \mbox{\em Proof.\hspace*{2mm}} From Lemma~\ref{contains_line} and Lemma~\ref{planar_pencil} (i), there is a line $l$ on $S$ containing $P$.
nodes.statement_short: Some $\mathbb F_q$-line on $S$ passes through $P$.

nodes.name: Justify the line
nodes.statement: Indeed the existence of an ${\Bbb F}_q$-line $l'$ on $S$ is guaranteed by Lemma~\ref{contains_line}; if the point $P$ in question lies on $l'$, there is nothing to do; when $P \not\in l'$, consider the ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane $H'$ containing $l'$ and $P$, then $S \cap H'$ is a planar ${\Bbb F}_q$-pencil by Lemma~\ref{planar_pencil} (i), which contains $P$; hence there is a line $l$ on $S$ containing $P$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $l'\subset S$ and the plane through $l'$ and $P$, which cuts a pencil containing $P$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Hence, by (ii) of Lemma~\ref{planar_pencil} there is a desired ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane, and such a plane is uniquely determined by $P$. \hfill \mbox{$ \Box $}
nodes.statement_short: The vertex bijection gives existence and uniqueness of $H$.

nodes.name: Section 4 setup: surface with (sqrt(q)^3+1)(q+1) points
nodes.statement: In this section, $q$ is assumed to be an even power of a prime number $p$ again, and $S$ is a surface in ${\Bbb P}^3$ of degree $\sqrt{q}+1$ defined over ${\Bbb F}_q$ without ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane components such that $N_q(S) = (\sqrt{q}^{3}+1)(q+1)$.
nodes.statement_short: $q$ an even prime power; $S$ of degree $\sqrt q+1$ without $\mathbb F_q$-planes with $(\sqrt q^3+1)(q+1)$ points.

nodes.name: N_q(S) attains both bounds
nodes.statement: Note that this number $N_q(S)$ achieves both the Weil-Deligne bound (\ref{weil_deligne}) for $n=3$ and the elementary bound (\ref{elementary_bound}).
conclusions: this number $N_q(S)$ achieves both the Weil-Deligne bound (\ref{weil_deligne}) for $n=3$ and the elementary bound (\ref{elementary_bound}).

nodes.name: Plane sections of S are pencils or Hermitian curves
assumptions: With the above situation, let $H$ be an ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane of ${\Bbb P}^3$.
conclusions: $S \cap H$ is a planar ${\Bbb F}_q$-pencil of degree $\sqrt{q}+1$, or
$S \cap H$ is a nonsingular Hermitian curve of degree $\sqrt{q}+1$ over ${\Bbb F}_q$.
nodes.statement_short: Each $\mathbb F_q$-plane section of $S$ is a planar pencil ($N_q(S)$ of them) or a nonsingular Hermitian curve ($\sqrt q^3(q+1)(\sqrt q-1)$ of them).
nodes.label: sqrt_q_plus_one_case

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.1
nodes.statement:
oindent \mbox{\em Proof.\hspace*{2mm}} Let $\check{\Bbb P}^3({\Bbb F}_q)$ denote the set of ${\Bbb F}_q$-planes of ${\Bbb P}^3$, and $\mathcal{P}_1$ the set of ${\Bbb F}_q$-planes having the property (1). The map $\mathcal{P}_1 
i H \mapsto v_{S \cap H} \in S({\Bbb F}_q)$ is bijective by Corollary~ef{bijective_pencil_point}. Hence $
u_1 = N_q(S)$. Let $\mathcal{P}_2= \check{\Bbb P}^3({\Bbb F}_q) \setminus \mathcal{P}_1 $. Note that if $H \in \mathcal{P}_2$, then $S \cap H$ has no ${\Bbb F}_q$-liner components by Lemma~ef{planar_pencil}~(i). Consider the correspondence \[ \mathcal{A} = \{(P, H) \mid P \in H\} \subset S({\Bbb F}_q) 	imes \check{\Bbb P}^3({\Bbb F}_q) \] with two projections $\pi_1: \mathcal{A} 	o S({\Bbb F}_q)$ and $\pi_2: \mathcal{A} 	o \check{\Bbb P}^3({\Bbb F}_q)$. Counting the cardinality of $\mathcal{A}$ by $\pi_1$, we have \[ {}^{\#}\mathcal{A} = N_q(S)\cdot(q^2+q+1). \] If $H \in \mathcal{P}_1$, then $ {}^{\#}\pi_2^{-1}(H) = N_q(S \cap H) = \sqrt{q}^3+q +1, $ and if $H \in \mathcal{P}_2$, then $ {}^{\#}\pi_2^{-1}(H) = N_q(S \cap H) \leq \sqrt{q}^3 +1 $ by (ef{sziklai_bound}). Hence, counting the cardinality of $\mathcal{A}$ by $\pi_2$, we have  egin{eqnarray*} {}^{\#}\mathcal{A} &\leq & N_q(S)\cdot (\sqrt{q}^3+q +1) + \left(  rac{q^4 -1}{q-1} -N_q(S) ight) (\sqrt{q}^3 +1)\ &=& N_q(S)\cdot(q^2+q+1). \end{eqnarray*} Therefore, if $H \in \mathcal{P}_2$, then $N_q(S \cap H) = \sqrt{q}^3 +1$. Furthermore, when $H \in \mathcal{P}_2$, since $S \cap H$ has no ${\Bbb F}_q$-line as a component, $S\cap H$ is a nonsingular Hermitian curve by (ef{hermitiancurve}) if $q 
eq 4$. We need a little more argument if $q=4$. We want to apply Lemma~ef{detour}. If an $\mathbb{F}_4$-point is not a flex of $S\cap H$, i.e., $i(T_P(S\cap H). S\cap H; P)=2$, then $T_P(S\cap H)$ meets with $S\cap H$ at exactly two $\mathbb{F}_4$-points, because $\deg S\cap H=3$. Consider all $\mathbb{F}_4$-planes $\{ H_{\lambda} \}$ in $\mathbb{P}^3$ such that $ H_{\lambda} \supset T_P(S\cap H_{\lambda}). $ Let $a = {}^{\#}\{ \lambda \mid H_{\lambda} \in \mathcal{P}_1 \}$. Then ${}^{\#}\{ \lambda \mid H_{\lambda} \in \mathcal{P}_2 \}= 5-a$. Since $N_4(S \cap H_{\lambda} )$ is either $13$ or $9$, we have $ 45 = (13-2)a +(9-2)(5-a) +2$. Hence there is an $\mathbb{F}_4$-plane $ H_{\lambda} $ such that $S \cap H_{\lambda}$ is a planar $\mathbb{F}_4$-pencil of degree $3$, and the line $T_{P}(S \cap H)$ lies on $H_{\lambda}$. But it is impossible, because any $\mathbb{F}_4$-line on $H_{\lambda}$ meets with the planar pencil at either $1$, or $3$, or $5$ points. \hfill \mbox{$ \Box $}
nodes.statement_short: Double counting of point-plane incidences forces non-pencil sections to have $\sqrt q^3+1$ points, so they are Hermitian by Hirschfeld-Storme-Thas-Voloch. For $q=4$ a tangent-plane count shows all points are flexes, so Lemma 2.3 applies.

nodes.name: Count pencil planes
nodes.statement:
oindent \mbox{\em Proof.\hspace*{2mm}} Let $\check{\Bbb P}^3({\Bbb F}_q)$ denote the set of ${\Bbb F}_q$-planes of ${\Bbb P}^3$, and $\mathcal{P}_1$ the set of ${\Bbb F}_q$-planes having the property (1). The map $\mathcal{P}_1 
i H \mapsto v_{S \cap H} \in S({\Bbb F}_q)$ is bijective by Corollary~ef{bijective_pencil_point}. Hence $
u_1 = N_q(S)$.
nodes.statement_short: Pencil planes biject with $S(\mathbb F_q)$ by Corollary 3.8.

nodes.name: Other planes have no lines
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{P}_2= \check{\Bbb P}^3({\Bbb F}_q) \setminus \mathcal{P}_1 $. Note that if $H \in \mathcal{P}_2$, then $S \cap H$ has no ${\Bbb F}_q$-liner components by Lemma~\ref{planar_pencil}~(i).
nodes.statement_short: Sections by the remaining planes have no $\mathbb F_q$-line components.

nodes.name: Incidence correspondence
nodes.statement: Consider the correspondence \[ \mathcal{A} = \{(P, H) \mid P \in H\} \subset S({\Bbb F}_q) \times \check{\Bbb P}^3({\Bbb F}_q) \] with two projections $\pi_1: \mathcal{A} \to S({\Bbb F}_q)$ and $\pi_2: \mathcal{A} \to \check{\Bbb P}^3({\Bbb F}_q)$. Counting the cardinality of $\mathcal{A}$ by $\pi_1$, we have \[ {}^{\#}\mathcal{A} = N_q(S)\cdot(q^2+q+1). \]
nodes.statement_short: Count point-plane incidences via the first projection.

nodes.name: Double counting
nodes.statement: If $H \in \mathcal{P}_1$, then $ {}^{\#}\pi_2^{-1}(H) = N_q(S \cap H) = \sqrt{q}^3+q +1, $ and if $H \in \mathcal{P}_2$, then $ {}^{\#}\pi_2^{-1}(H) = N_q(S \cap H) \leq \sqrt{q}^3 +1 $ by (\ref{sziklai_bound}). Hence, counting the cardinality of $\mathcal{A}$ by $\pi_2$, we have \begin{eqnarray*} {}^{\#}\mathcal{A} &\leq & N_q(S)\cdot (\sqrt{q}^3+q +1) + \left( \frac{q^4 -1}{q-1} -N_q(S) \right) (\sqrt{q}^3 +1)\\ &=& N_q(S)\cdot(q^2+q+1). \end{eqnarray*} Therefore, if $H \in \mathcal{P}_2$, then $N_q(S \cap H) = \sqrt{q}^3 +1$.
nodes.statement_short: Counting via the second projection with the Sziklai bound forces $N_q(S\cap H)=\sqrt q^3+1$ on $\mathcal P_2$.

nodes.name: Hermitian for q != 4
nodes.statement: Furthermore, when $H \in \mathcal{P}_2$, since $S \cap H$ has no ${\Bbb F}_q$-line as a component, $S\cap H$ is a nonsingular Hermitian curve by (\ref{hermitiancurve}) if $q \neq 4$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the Hirschfeld-Storme-Thas-Voloch theorem.

nodes.name: Case q = 4
nodes.statement: We need a little more argument if $q=4$. We want to apply Lemma~\ref{detour}. If an $\mathbb{F}_4$-point is not a flex of $S\cap H$, i.e., $i(T_P(S\cap H). S\cap H; P)=2$, then $T_P(S\cap H)$ meets with $S\cap H$ at exactly two $\mathbb{F}_4$-points, because $\deg S\cap H=3$. Consider all $\mathbb{F}_4$-planes $\{ H_{\lambda} \}$ in $\mathbb{P}^3$ such that $ H_{\lambda} \supset T_P(S\cap H_{\lambda}). $ Let $a = {}^{\#}\{ \lambda \mid H_{\lambda} \in \mathcal{P}_1 \}$. Then ${}^{\#}\{ \lambda \mid H_{\lambda} \in \mathcal{P}_2 \}= 5-a$. Since $N_4(S \cap H_{\lambda} )$ is either $13$ or $9$, we have $ 45 = (13-2)a +(9-2)(5-a) +2$. Hence there is an $\mathbb{F}_4$-plane $ H_{\lambda} $ such that $S \cap H_{\lambda}$ is a planar $\mathbb{F}_4$-pencil of degree $3$, and the line $T_{P}(S \cap H)$ lies on $H_{\lambda}$. But it is impossible, because any $\mathbb{F}_4$-line on $H_{\lambda}$ meets with the planar pencil at either $1$, or $3$, or $5$ points. \hfill \mbox{$ \Box $}
nodes.statement_short: For $q=4$, show every point is a flex and apply Lemma 2.3.

nodes.name: Plan for q=4
nodes.statement: We need a little more argument if $q=4$. We want to apply Lemma~\ref{detour}.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to Lemma 2.3.

nodes.name: Non-flex tangent
nodes.statement: If an $\mathbb{F}_4$-point is not a flex of $S\cap H$, i.e., $i(T_P(S\cap H). S\cap H; P)=2$, then $T_P(S\cap H)$ meets with $S\cap H$ at exactly two $\mathbb{F}_4$-points, because $\deg S\cap H=3$.
nodes.statement_short: A non-flex tangent meets the cubic in exactly two points.

nodes.name: Planes through the tangent
nodes.statement: Consider all $\mathbb{F}_4$-planes $\{ H_{\lambda} \}$ in $\mathbb{P}^3$ such that $ H_{\lambda} \supset T_P(S\cap H_{\lambda}). $ Let $a = {}^{\#}\{ \lambda \mid H_{\lambda} \in \mathcal{P}_1 \}$.
nodes.statement_short: Consider the five planes through the tangent line; $a$ of them are pencil planes.

nodes.name: Count
nodes.statement: Then ${}^{\#}\{ \lambda \mid H_{\lambda} \in \mathcal{P}_2 \}= 5-a$. Since $N_4(S \cap H_{\lambda} )$ is either $13$ or $9$, we have $ 45 = (13-2)a +(9-2)(5-a) +2$.
nodes.statement_short: Counting points gives $45=11a+7(5-a)+2$.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: Hence there is an $\mathbb{F}_4$-plane $ H_{\lambda} $ such that $S \cap H_{\lambda}$ is a planar $\mathbb{F}_4$-pencil of degree $3$, and the line $T_{P}(S \cap H)$ lies on $H_{\lambda}$. But it is impossible, because any $\mathbb{F}_4$-line on $H_{\lambda}$ meets with the planar pencil at either $1$, or $3$, or $5$ points. \hfill \mbox{$ \Box $}
nodes.statement_short: The tangent line would lie in a pencil plane, impossible by intersection counts.

nodes.name: Last step of the proof of Theorem 1.2
nodes.statement_short: Normalize coordinates using a Hermitian section $H_\infty$ and the pencil planes through its tangent lines, then force the equation into Hermitian form term by term. The key step: $g_2$ would have $q-1$ linear factors $X_0-\lambda X_1$, exceeding its degree.

nodes.name: Hermitian section
nodes.statement: \noindent \mbox{\em Last Step of the Proof of Theorem~\ref{maintheorem}.\hspace*{2mm}} From Proposition~\ref{sqrt_q_plus_one_case}, there is an ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane $H_{\infty} \subset {\Bbb P}^3$ such that $S \cap H_{\infty}$ is a nonsingular Hermitian curve.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 4.1 gives a plane $H_\infty$ cutting a nonsingular Hermitian curve.

nodes.name: Coordinates
nodes.statement: Choose a system of homogeneous coordinates $X_0, X_1, X_2, X_3$ of ${\Bbb P}^3$ such that \begin{enumerate}[(i)] \item $H_{\infty}$ is given by $X_0=0$; and \item the plane curve $S \cap H_{\infty}$ in $H_{\infty}={\Bbb P}^2$ is given by \[ \bar{X}_1 \bar{X}_2^{\sqrt{q}} + \bar{X}_1^{\sqrt{q}} \bar{X}_2 + \bar{X}_3^{\sqrt{q}+1} =0, \] where $\bar{X}_1, \bar{X}_2, \bar{X}_3$ are coordinates on $H_{\infty}$ induced by $X_1, X_2, X_3$ respectively. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Choose coordinates with $H_\infty=\{X_0=0\}$ and the section in standard form.

nodes.name: Coordinate choice
nodes.statement: Choose a system of homogeneous coordinates $X_0, X_1, X_2, X_3$ of ${\Bbb P}^3$ such that
nodes.statement_short: Choose homogeneous coordinates such that the following hold.

nodes.name: Item (i)
nodes.statement: $H_{\infty}$ is given by $X_0=0$; and

nodes.name: Item (ii)
nodes.statement: the plane curve $S \cap H_{\infty}$ in $H_{\infty}={\Bbb P}^2$ is given by \[ \bar{X}_1 \bar{X}_2^{\sqrt{q}} + \bar{X}_1^{\sqrt{q}} \bar{X}_2 + \bar{X}_3^{\sqrt{q}+1} =0, \] where $\bar{X}_1, \bar{X}_2, \bar{X}_3$ are coordinates on $H_{\infty}$ induced by $X_1, X_2, X_3$ respectively. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: The section $S\cap H_\infty$ is $\bar X_1\bar X_2^{\sqrt q}+\bar X_1^{\sqrt q}\bar X_2+\bar X_3^{\sqrt q+1}=0$.

nodes.name: Tangent lines
nodes.statement: Let $P_1=(0,0,1,0)$ and $P_2=(0,1,0,0)$, both of which are points on $S \cap H_{\infty}$. For $\alpha = 1, 2$, the tangent line $L_{\alpha}$ at $P_{\alpha}$ to $S\cap H_{\infty}$ in $H_{\infty}={\Bbb P}^2$ is given by $\bar{X}_{\alpha}=0$. It is easy to see that $S \cap L_{\alpha}= \{ P_{\alpha} \}$.
nodes.statement_short: Tangent lines $L_\alpha$ at $P_\alpha$ meet $S$ only at $P_\alpha$.

nodes.name: Unique pencil plane through L_alpha
nodes.statement: Hence for an ${\Bbb F}_q$-plane $H \supset L_{\alpha}$, \[ {}^{\#} \left( S({\Bbb F}_q) \cap (H \setminus L_{\alpha}) \right) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ccl} \sqrt{q}^3 + 1 -1 & & \mbox{\rm if $S\cap H$ is Hermitian}\\ \sqrt{q}^3 +q +1 -1& & \mbox{\rm if $S\cap H$ is an ${\Bbb F}_q$-pencil}. \end{array} \right. \] Counting the number $N_q(S) -1$ by using all ${\Bbb F}_q$-planes containing $L_{\alpha}$, we know that there is a unique plane $H_{\alpha, 0} \supset L_{\alpha}$ such that $S \cap H_{\alpha, 0}$ is a planar ${\Bbb F}_q$-pencil of degree $\sqrt{q}+1$; and $S \cap H_{\alpha, \lambda }$ is a nonsingular Hermitian curve for other plane $H_{\alpha, \lambda} \supset L_{\alpha}$.
nodes.statement_short: Counting shows exactly one plane through $L_\alpha$ cuts a pencil.

nodes.name: Normalize pencil planes
nodes.statement: By changing coordinates of type \[ \left\{ \begin{array}{ccc} X_1 & \mapsto & X_1 + a X_0 \\ X_2 & \mapsto & X_2 + b X_0 \end{array} \right. \] if necessary, we may suppose that $H_{\alpha, 0}$ is defined by $X_{\alpha}=0$ for $\alpha =1$ and $2$ respectively. But the situation on $H_{\infty}$ never change.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG the pencil planes are $X_1=0$ and $X_2=0$.

nodes.name: Form of F
nodes.statement: Summing up, $S$ is defined by \[ F(X_0, \dots , X_3) = X_0 f(X_0, \dots , X_3) + h(X_1, X_2, X_3) =0 \] where \[ h(X_1, X_2, X_3)= X_1 X_2^{\sqrt{q}} + X_1^{\sqrt{q}}X_2 + X_3^{\sqrt{q}+1} \] and $\deg f = \sqrt{q}$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $F=X_0f+h$ with $h$ the Hermitian curve's form.

nodes.name: Monomial constraints
nodes.statement: Since $S \cap H_{1, 0} = S \cap \{ X_1 = 0 \}$ is a planar ${\Bbb F}_q$-pencil with the vertex $P_1= (0,0,1,0)$, \[ F(X_0, 0, X_2 , X_3) = X_0 f(X_0, 0, X_2 , X_3) + X_3^{\sqrt{q}+1} \] does not contain $X_2$, because this polynomial must have the form $ c \prod_j (X_0+\gamma_j X_3),$ with $c \in {\Bbb F}_q^{\ast}.$ Hence, in $F(X_0, X_1, X_2, X_3)$, any monomial containing $X_2$ also contains $X_1$. By the same argument on $S \cap H_{2, 0} =S \cap \{ X_2 = 0 \}$, any monomial containing $X_1$ also contains $X_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Pencil sections force $X_1$ and $X_2$ to appear together.

nodes.name: Decompose f
nodes.statement: Therefore $f(X_0, X_1, X_2, X_3)$ is written as \[ f(X_0, X_1, X_2, X_3) = g_1(X_0, X_3) + g_2(X_0, \dots , X_3)X_1X_2, \] where $\deg g_1 = \sqrt{q}$ and $\deg g_2 = \sqrt{q}-2$.

nodes.name: Hermitian sections H_{1,lambda}
nodes.statement: For the plane $H_{1, \lambda} = \{X_0 = \lambda X_1 \} \ (\lambda \in {\Bbb F}_q^{\ast}),$ since $S \cap \{X_0 = \lambda X_1 \}$ is a Hermitian curve, \begin{eqnarray} \lefteqn{ \rho F(\lambda X_1, X_1, X_2, X_3)=}\nonumber \\ && \rho \left( \lambda X_1 (g_1(\lambda X_1, X_3) + g_2(\lambda X_1, X_1, X_2, X_3)X_1 X_2) + h(X_1, X_2, X_3) \right) \end{eqnarray} is a Hermitian polynomial for some $\rho \in {\Bbb F}_q^{\ast}$. Since $X_3^{\sqrt{q}+1}$ appears only in $h(X_1, X_2, X_3)$, the constant $\rho$ must be an element of ${\Bbb F}_{\sqrt{q}}^{\ast}$. Hence (\ref{polynomialinproblem}) is a Hermitian polynomial even if $\rho =1$. Since $h$ itself Hermitian, \[ \lambda g_1(\lambda X_1, X_3)X_1 + \lambda g_2(\lambda X_1, X_1, X_2, X_3)X_1^2 X_2 \] must be Hermitian.
nodes.statement_short: Sections by $X_0=\lambda X_1$ are Hermitian, so the residual part of $F$ must be Hermitian.

nodes.name: g_2 vanishes
nodes.statement: Any monomial in $g_2(\lambda X_1, X_1, X_2, X_3)X_1^2 X_2$ never appear in $g_1(\lambda X_1, X_3)X_1$. So $g_2(\lambda X_1, X_1, X_2, X_3))X_1^2 X_2$ contains the monomials only of types $X_i^{\sqrt{q}+1}$ or $X_i^{\sqrt{q}}X_j$. Hence \[ g_2(\lambda X_1, X_1, X_2, X_3)X_1^2 X_2 = \mu X_1^{\sqrt{q}} X_2 \ (\mu \in {\Bbb F}_q). \] But the monomial $X_1X_2^{\sqrt{q}+1}$ can't appear in \[ g_1(\lambda X_1, X_3)X_1 + g_2(\lambda X_1, X_1, X_2, X_3)X_1^2 X_2. \] Hence $ g_2(\lambda X_1, X_1, X_2, X_3) =0$, that is, $X_0 - \lambda X_1$ is a factor of $g_2(X_0, X_1, X_2, X_3)$ for any $\lambda \in {\Bbb F}_q^{\ast}$. But $\deg g_2 = \sqrt{q}-2 \, (< q-1)$, it is impossible. Therefore $g_2(X_0, X_1, X_2, X_3) =0$ and $\lambda g_1(\lambda X_1, X_3)X_1 $ is Hermitian.
nodes.statement_short: Monomial analysis gives $X_0-\lambda X_1\mid g_2$ for all $\lambda$, impossible by degree, so $g_2=0$.

nodes.name: Determine g_1
nodes.statement: Let \[ g_1(X_0, X_3) = \sum_{i=0}^{\sqrt{q}} a_i X_0^{i}X_3^{\sqrt{q}-i}. \] Then \[ \lambda g_1(\lambda X_1, X_3) X_1= \sum_{i=0}^{\sqrt{q}} a_i \lambda^{i+1} X_1^{i+1}X_3^{\sqrt{q}-i}, \] which is Hermitian. Hence $a_i = 0$ for $i \neq 0, \, \sqrt{q}-1, \, \sqrt{q}$; and also $a_0^{\sqrt{q}} = a_{\sqrt{q}-1}$ and $a_{\sqrt{q}} \in {\Bbb F}_{\sqrt{q}}$, that is, \[ g_1(X_0, X_3) = a_0 X_3^{\sqrt{q}} + a_0^{\sqrt{q}}X_0^{\sqrt{q}-1}X_3 + a_{\sqrt{q}}X_0^{\sqrt{q}} \ \mbox{\rm with $a_{\sqrt{q}} \in {\Bbb F}_{\sqrt{q}}$}. \] Hence \[ F(X_0, \dots , X_3) = a_0 X_0 X_3^{\sqrt{q}} + a_0^{\sqrt{q}}X_0^{\sqrt{q}}X_3 + a_{\sqrt{q}}X_0^{\sqrt{q}+1} +h(X_1, X_2, X_3), \] which is Hermitian.
nodes.statement_short: Hermitian condition forces $g_1=a_0X_3^{\sqrt q}+a_0^{\sqrt q}X_0^{\sqrt q-1}X_3+a_{\sqrt q}X_0^{\sqrt q}$.

nodes.name: Nonsingularity
nodes.statement: If $a_{\sqrt{q}} =0$, then the surface is a cone of a nonsingular Hermitian curve with vertex $(1,0,0,0)$, and then $N_q(S) = (\sqrt{q}^3 +1)q +1$, which is not the given number. So $a_{\sqrt{q}} \in {\Bbb F}_{\sqrt{q}}^{\ast}$, and hence $S$ is a nonsingular Hermitian surface. \hfill \mbox{$ \Box $}
nodes.statement_short: $a_{\sqrt q}=0$ gives a cone with the wrong point count, so $S$ is nonsingular Hermitian.

nodes.name: Restricted polynomial on H_{1,lambda}
nodes.statement: \lefteqn{ \rho F(\lambda X_1, X_1, X_2, X_3)=}\nonumber \\ && \rho \left( \lambda X_1 (g_1(\lambda X_1, X_3) + g_2(\lambda X_1, X_1, X_2, X_3)X_1 X_2) + h(X_1, X_2, X_3) \right)
nodes.label: polynomialinproblem

nodes.name: Rück-Stichtenoth theorem
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a nonsingular curve of genus $g= \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{q}(\sqrt{q}-1)$ defined over ${\Bbb F}_q$. If $N_q(C) = \sqrt{q}^3 +1$, then the function field $\mathbb{F}_q(C)$ of $C$ coincides with that of the Hermitian curve over $\mathbb{F}_q$.
assumptions: Let $C$ be a nonsingular curve of genus $g= \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{q}(\sqrt{q}-1)$ defined over ${\Bbb F}_q$.
If $N_q(C) = \sqrt{q}^3 +1$,
conclusions: then the function field $\mathbb{F}_q(C)$ of $C$ coincides with that of the Hermitian curve over $\mathbb{F}_q$.
nodes.statement_short: A nonsingular curve of genus $\sqrt q(\sqrt q-1)/2$ with $\sqrt q^3+1$ points has the Hermitian function field.
nodes.label: RStheorem

nodes.name: Rück-Stichtenoth implies Hirschfeld et al. for nonsingular plane curves
nodes.statement: If one considers only nonsingular plane curves, R\"{u}ck-Stichtenoth's characterization implies Hirschfeld et al.'s, because the linear system $g_{\sqrt{q}+1}^2$ is unique if $g= \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{q}(\sqrt{q}-1) > 1$. When $q=4$, the genus in question is $1$. As was mentioned in \cite{hir-sto-tha-vol}, the plane curve $\{X_0 + \omega X_1 + \omega^2 X_2=0\}$ over $\mathbb{F}_4$ is not Hermitian, but has $9$ $\mathbb{F}_4$-points, where $\mathbb{F}_4 = \{0, 1, \omega , \omega^2\}$. However the function field of this curve over $\mathbb{F}_4$ coincides with that of the Hermitian curve over $\mathbb{F}_4$.
nodes.statement_short: For nonsingular plane curves, Rück-Stichtenoth implies Hirschfeld et al.; for $q=4$ a non-Hermitian cubic with 9 points still has the Hermitian function field.

nodes.name: Reinterpretation of the Rück-Stichtenoth theorem via zeta functions
nodes.statement: Since the number $\sqrt{q}^3 +1$ achieves the Weil bound for $g= \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{q}(\sqrt{q}-1) $, the zeta function of the nonsingular curve $C$ in (A.\ref{RStheorem}) is $\frac{(1+\sqrt{q}t)^{2g}}{(1-t)(1-qt)}$. So Theorem~A.\ref{RStheorem} can be interpreted as:
nodes.statement_short: Attaining the Weil bound determines the zeta function, so Theorem A.1 can be restated in terms of zeta functions.

nodes.name: Rück-Stichtenoth theorem (zeta-function form)
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a nonsingular curve of genus $g= \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{q}(\sqrt{q}-1) >1$ defined over ${\Bbb F}_q$ whose zeta function is $\frac{(1+\sqrt{q}t)^{2g}}{(1-t)(1-qt)}$. Then $C$ is the Hermitian curve.
assumptions: Let $C$ be a nonsingular curve of genus $g= \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{q}(\sqrt{q}-1) >1$ defined over ${\Bbb F}_q$ whose zeta function is $\frac{(1+\sqrt{q}t)^{2g}}{(1-t)(1-qt)}$.
conclusions: Then $C$ is the Hermitian curve.

nodes.name: Zeta function of the Hermitian surface
nodes.statement: On the other hand, the number of ${\Bbb F}_q$-points of the Hermitian surface attains the Weil-Deligne bound, and its zeta function is: \begin{equation} \frac{1}{(1-t)(1-qt)^{b_2}(1-q^2t)} \ \ \ \ \ (b_2 =q\sqrt{q} -q + \sqrt{q} + 1). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Zeta function of the Hermitian surface (formula)
nodes.label: zetaofhermitian

nodes.name: Is a surface with the Hermitian zeta function Hermitian?
nodes.statement: It is natural to ask whether a nonsingular surface over ${\Bbb F}_q$ with the zeta function (\ref{zetaofhermitian}) is Hermitian or not.

nodes.name: zeta function Z_X(t)
nodes.statement: From now on, when $X$ is a nonsingular surface over ${\Bbb F}_q$, $Z_X(t)$ denotes the zeta function of $X$.

nodes.name: Zeta function of a blow-up at a rational point
nodes.statement: Let $\Tilde{X}$ be a blowing-up of a nonsingular surface $X$ over ${\Bbb F}_q$ with center an ${\Bbb F}_q$-point of $X$. Then $ Z_{\Tilde{X}}(t) = Z_X(t) \frac{1}{(1-qt)}. $
assumptions: Let $\Tilde{X}$ be a blowing-up of a nonsingular surface $X$ over ${\Bbb F}_q$ with center an ${\Bbb F}_q$-point of $X$.
conclusions: Z_{\Tilde{X}}(t) = Z_X(t) \frac{1}{(1-qt)}.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.4
nodes.statement: \noindent \mbox{\em Proof.\hspace*{2mm}} Let $N_m(X)$ and $N_m(\Tilde{X})$ denote the number of ${\Bbb F}_{q^m}$-points of $X$ and $\Tilde{X}$ respectively. Then $N_m(\Tilde{X})= N_m(X) +q^m$. Hence \begin{align*} Z_{\Tilde{X}}(t) &= \exp \left( \sum_{m=1}^{\infty} (N_m(X) + q^m)\frac{t^m}{m} \right)\\ &= \exp \left(\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}N_m(X)\frac{t^m}{m}\right) \exp\left(\sum_{m=1}^{\infty} q^m \frac{t^m}{m} \right)\\ &= Z_X(t) \frac{1}{(1-qt)}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Blowing up adds $q^m$ points over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$; exponentiate the generating series.

nodes.name: Point counts of the blow-up
nodes.statement: \noindent \mbox{\em Proof.\hspace*{2mm}} Let $N_m(X)$ and $N_m(\Tilde{X})$ denote the number of ${\Bbb F}_{q^m}$-points of $X$ and $\Tilde{X}$ respectively. Then $N_m(\Tilde{X})= N_m(X) +q^m$.
nodes.statement_short: $N_m(\tilde X)=N_m(X)+q^m$.

nodes.name: Zeta computation
nodes.statement: Hence \begin{align*} Z_{\Tilde{X}}(t) &= \exp \left( \sum_{m=1}^{\infty} (N_m(X) + q^m)\frac{t^m}{m} \right)\\ &= \exp \left(\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}N_m(X)\frac{t^m}{m}\right) \exp\left(\sum_{m=1}^{\infty} q^m \frac{t^m}{m} \right)\\ &= Z_X(t) \frac{1}{(1-qt)}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Split the exponential to get the factor $1/(1-qt)$.

nodes.name: Iterated blow-ups of P^2 with the Hermitian zeta function
nodes.statement: Let $X_1 = {\Bbb P}^2$ over ${\Bbb F}_q$. It is obvious that $ Z_{X_1}(t) = \frac{1}{(1-t)(1-qt)(1-q^2t)}. $ Define a nonsingular surface $X_n$ over ${\Bbb F}_q$ by a blowing-up of $X_{n-1}$ with center an ${\Bbb F}_{q}$-point, successively. Then the zeta function of $X_{b_2}$ is the same as Hermitian surface's. However, if $\sqrt{q}+1 \geq 4$, the Hermitian surface of degree $\sqrt{q}+1$ is not rational. So, if $q>2^2$, then the function field of $X_{b_2}$ does not coincides with that of the Hermitian surface over ${\Bbb F}_q$.
nodes.statement_short: Blowing up $\mathbb P^2$ at $b_2-1$ rational points gives the Hermitian surface's zeta function, but for $q>4$ a rational, hence non-Hermitian, surface.

nodes.name: Blow-up surface is not Hermitian
nodes.statement: So, if $q>2^2$, then the function field of $X_{b_2}$ does not coincides with that of the Hermitian surface over ${\Bbb F}_q$.
conclusions: then the function field of $X_{b_2}$ does not coincides with that of the Hermitian surface over ${\Bbb F}_q$.
